alalal-e76991-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 2: whether faith is a virtue.

alalal-e76991-d1e111.summary: States the second preliminary question: whether faith is a virtue.

alalal-e76991-d1e118.summary: First objection: Cicero defines virtue as a voluntary habit acting like nature, in accord with reason; faith is not in the will, nor does it incline like nature, since it is a kind of cognition.

alalal-e76991-d1e146.summary: Second objection: the Philosopher says virtue concerns passions and operations and produces the best; faith concerns neither, but rests on truth.

alalal-e76991-d1e173.summary: Third objection: the end of the speculative intellect is truth and of the practical, work; faith's end is truth, so it is in the speculative intellect, where there is no virtue.

alalal-e76991-d1e202.summary: Fourth objection: faith cannot be in the intellect as consequent on the will, since cognition precedes every movement of affect; faith announces divine things and opens the eye, so it is prior to affect and purely cognitive, and pure cognition is not virtue since it is not from us but compelled by truth.

alalal-e76991-d1e239.summary: Rejects the reply that faith is of truth under the aspect of good and so in the practical intellect: then truth would be material and good formal, and faith would differ from charity only materially, which is false.

alalal-e76991-d1e261.summary: Rejects the reply that truth is the good of the rational power: every power, however speculative, has an end that is its good, so every science would be a virtue.

alalal-e76991-d1e290.summary: Sed contra: a habit moving a power not as art or science but as nature is a virtue (Cicero); art and science rest on reasons, faith does not, so it moves like nature, as heavy things fall.

alalal-e76991-d1e322.summary: Second sed contra: virtue is the disposition of the perfect to the best (Aristotle), and faith orders all it perfects to the best, God.
concepts: virtue as disposition to the best

alalal-e76991-d1e335.summary: Third sed contra: whatever principle justifies and purifies the heart is a virtue, since only virtue is formally contrary to the impurity of sin; faith purifies hearts (Acts 15:9), justifies (Augustine), and is a seal of justice (Romans 4:11).

alalal-e76991-d1e364.summary: Fourth sed contra: Augustine calls faith a virtue, as cited in Lombard's text.

alalal-e76991-d1e371.summary: Fifth sed contra: Scripture throughout praises faith, as Hebrews 11:6, Ecclesiasticus 45:4 and the woman healed in Luke 8:48.

alalal-e76991-d1e391.summary: Solution: faith is a theological virtue. Theological virtues order immediately to God, as cardinal virtues order to the mean in passions and operations. The rectitude of cardinal virtues lies in the mean, their deviation in excess or defect; that of theological virtues lies in right order to the end, beatitude as true, good, unfailing and arduous, their deviation in turning from the end to mutable good.
claims: Faith is a theological virtue, ordering immediately to God.
Theological virtues' rectitude lies in right order to the final end, not in a mean.

alalal-e76991-d1e435.summary: Reply to the first objection: virtue is 'voluntary' not because every virtue is in the will but because the will moves its operation and the generation of the habit; in infused virtues the will at least cooperates by consent. Faith inclines like nature because it lacks sufficient reason for assent and, even if it had one, does not rest on it: in science reason precedes assent, but in faith one first assents to first truth for its own sake and then seeks reasons to understand what is believed, still not resting on them. So the assent of faith proceeds entirely from the freedom of the will.
claims: In faith, assent to first truth precedes the search for reasons and never rests on them.
The assent of faith proceeds from the freedom of the will and so inclines like nature.

alalal-e76991-d1e488.summary: Reply to the second objection: the Philosopher speaks of political and moral virtues, not intellectual ones, for which he gives a different account in Ethics VI. Or faith has an interior operation, tending to first truth, in which it achieves the best, though it has no passions, since not every virtue concerns passions.

alalal-e76991-d1e521.summary: Reply to the third objection: there is truth as the end of speculation, the universal ratio of a thing moving the intellect, and truth that beatifies the intellect, outside it, the supreme reality and light of eternal felicity, the end of an intellect moved by affect. Albert concedes that the 'truth under the aspect of good' reply fails, since faith rests on first truth for its own sake. The Philosopher's 'truth' is equivocal with faith's end.
claims: Faith's object is first truth as beatifying reality, not truth as the ratio of things known speculatively.
Faith rests on first truth for its own sake, not under the aspect of good.

alalal-e76991-d1e567.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: what follows the will is consent, the substance of the act of faith, which comes after some cognition to which the will tends; the reception of the credible through hearing precedes affect, but that is only understanding what the name signifies, not a reason proving that or why it is so, and the will freely consents.
claims: Only grasping what the words of faith signify precedes the will; the assent itself follows the will.

alalal-e76991-d1e602.summary: A subtler distinction: the intellect as intellect has no virtue; as extended to work it is practical, either because affect directs inquiry into operables or because its form is a principle of work, and here are the intellectual virtues such as prudence and understanding. There is also an intellect of truth whose consent is moved by the will, the affective intellect, in which faith resides; though one in subject, these differ in being and ratio.
claims: Faith resides in the affective intellect, whose consent to truth is moved by the will.

alalal-e76991.summary: Article 2 asks whether faith is a virtue. Objections argue that faith is cognitive, not voluntary or natural in its inclination; that it concerns neither passions nor operations; that it resides in the speculative intellect, which has no virtues; and that cognition precedes affect, so faith is not from us. Attempts to place faith in the practical intellect by treating truth as good are rejected. Albert holds that faith is a theological virtue, ordering immediately to God, with rectitude defined by order to the final end rather than by a mean. Its assent comes from the free will, and it inclines like nature because it does not rest on reasons: the believer first assents to first truth for its own sake and then seeks understanding. Its object is the beatifying first truth, not speculative truth. Only grasping what the words mean precedes the will. Faith resides in the 'affective intellect', whose consent is moved by the will, distinct in ratio from both the speculative and the practical intellect.
claims: Faith is a theological virtue, ordering immediately to God.
The assent of faith proceeds from the freedom of the will and does not rest on reasons, even when reasons are found.
Faith's object is first truth as beatifying reality, held for its own sake, not truth under the aspect of good.
Faith resides in the affective intellect, whose consent is moved by the will.
